title: What should you ask first in a pricing case, and which trap should you avoid?
description: The first question to ask in a pricing case, how to structure it, and the trap to avoid.
hook: Ask first what the product is worth to the customer, because value sets the ceiling on price and cost only sets the floor. The trap is using just one lens (usually cost or competitors) and naming a price without saying how many units you expect to sell at it.
body:
The first question to ask

What is the product worth to the customer, compared with their next best option?

Pricing cases have no single right answer, which can feel unsettling. Value to the customer is the best place to start because it is the upper limit: nobody pays more than the product saves or earns them, or more than their next best alternative costs. Then ask two practical questions: what are the costs, and what is the client trying to achieve (volume, margin, or market share)?

How to build your structure

  • Floor: variable cost per unit, plus the fixed costs to recover.
  • Ceiling: value to the customer; price of their next best option.
  • Reference: competitor prices and substitutes.
  • Choose: penetration or skimming; volume at each price; effect on the client's other products.

The final price sits somewhere between floor and ceiling. Where exactly depends on competition and the client's goal. See the three ways to set a price for more on each lens, and the pricing framework for the full tree.

Test a price rise against lost volume

A cinema charges $10 a ticket. Each extra visitor costs $3 to serve, so contribution is $7 a ticket. It sells 100,000 tickets, for $700k of contribution before fixed costs. Management wants to raise the price to $12.

At $12, contribution is $9 a ticket. To keep $700k, the cinema needs $700k ÷ $9 ≈ 77,800 tickets. It can lose about 22% of its visitors and still break even on the rise.

But cinemas also earn on food and drink. Suppose each visitor brings $4 of food and drink contribution. Contribution per visitor is then $11 today ($7 + $4) and $13 after the rise ($9 + $4). Total today is 100,000 × $11 = $1.1M, and break-even is $1.1M ÷ $13 ≈ 84,600 visitors. Now the cinema can only afford to lose about 15%. The second lens changed the answer.

So the recommendation is not just a number. It names who is most price-sensitive (students, families, weekday visitors), what competitors charge, and how to test it: for example, raise weekend prices first, when the cinema is full, and watch attendance. More on demand response in price elasticity explained.

The trap most people fall into

Using one lens and skipping volume. "Cost is $3, so charge $6" ignores what customers will pay. "Competitors charge $11, so charge $11" ignores whether the product is better or worse. And any price without a volume estimate cannot be compared with another.

Weak: "Competitors charge around $12, so I'd raise the price to $12."
Strong: "At $12 we can lose up to about 15% of visitors and still break even, once you include food and drink. Weekends are full, so I'd raise weekend prices first and check whether attendance holds."

Two prompts to try

Should a streaming service launch a cheaper plan with ads?

Show the answer
  • New subscribers: people who find the full price too high; win-back of those who left.
  • Downgrades: current subscribers switching to the cheaper plan; revenue lost per switch.
  • Ad revenue: ads per hour and what advertisers pay; effect on the viewing experience.
  • Capability: ad sales team and technology; content rights that allow ads.

Where to start: downgrades. Ad revenue per viewer must make up for every subscriber who switches down.

The trap: counting only the new subscribers.

What should a start-up charge for a smart thermostat that cuts heating bills?

Show the answer
  • Floor: hardware, installation and support cost per unit.
  • Ceiling: yearly savings on the customer's heating bill, and how many years they will count.
  • Reference: rival thermostats and what energy suppliers offer free or subsidised.
  • Model: one-off price, subscription, or a share of savings; sales through installers or direct.

Where to start: the ceiling. If it saves $150 a year and buyers want their money back within two years, the price ceiling is about $300.

The trap: pricing at cost plus a margin and leaving value on the table.
